title: They gave birth in the south. Now, they're helping Inuit deliver closer to home
summary: Margaret Tukkiapik and Kayla Annanack-Lauzon study through the Puvirnituq Inuulitsivik Health Centre's midwifery program to provide prenatal, labour and post-natal care for Inuit who would otherwise…

image.caption: Midwife trainee Kayla Annanack-Lauzon, left, and Margaret Tukkiapik, right, study through the Puvirnituq Inuulitsivik Health Centre's midwifery program to provide prenatal, labour and post-natal care for Inuit who would otherwise travel outside of their region, culture and language. (Josianne Letour

blocks.text: Margaret Tukkiapik's hands are peppered with some of the accomplishments of her work.
Small circular tattoos line each one of her fingers — representing every umbilical cord she's cut in her time assisting labouring mothers.
"I'm missing a few dots," said Tukkiapik, holding up her hands proudly.
The midwife at the Ungava Tulattavik Health Centre's maternity ward, who has attended 95 births, jokes that the stick-and-poke tattoos can be quite painful.

In Inuit traditions, cutting the cord of a baby is an honour and a responsibility — marking the start of a special relationship with the child, who is referred to as the cord-cutter's arnaliaq, if the baby is a girl, or angusiaq, for a boy.
Tukkiapik has 10 of each.

Margaret Tukkiapik was a self-taught doula before starting to study as a midwife five years ago. She gets a marking on her fingers every time she cuts a baby's umbilical cord. (Josianne Letourneau/CBC)
"As they're cutting the cord, they will install values in the child," she said.
As they grow, the children present their accomplishments — their first sewing project, fish or caribou — back to the person who cut their cord, says Tukkiapik.
Tukkiapik's arnaliaqs and angusiaqs are part of what pushed her into midwifery in her home community of Kuujjuaq, Que.

items: 746 births over 36 years: Inuk midwife long served her remote community

blocks.text: She was a self-taught doula for years before she started studying through Puvirnituq's Inuulitsivik Health Centre midwifery program — now celebrating its 40th year in operation.
This month, Tukkiapik passed her exam after training for five years.

She joins the ranks of other Inuit midwives who have stepped up to provide safe options for pregnant Inuit who would otherwise have to fly south to deliver outside of their region, culture and language.
Inside the northern maternity unit helping pregnant Inuit deliver close to home
A 'night and day' difference
For Kayla Annanack-Lauzon, a midwife in training, this mission is personal.

She's edging closer to her due date with her second baby, and plans to deliver in Kuujjuaq. But she can't help but compare this pregnancy to her first — when she had most of her prenatal follow-ups and delivery in Montreal.
"There's really been a difference, like between night and day," she said.
"I'm able to be served in my language at home and not going into … a big crazy hospital that I'm not familiar with."
Kayla Annanack-Lauzon, left, will deliver her second child in December, in the same maternity ward where she currently works as a midwife. (Josianne Letourneau/CBC)

After studying nursing, Annanack-Lauzon began training with the Inuulitsivik midwifery program in May, and has attended four births. She says patients "always have something good to say about their experience when they compare it to the South."
But up north, there's no continuous monitoring, epidural or inductions, notes Tukkiapik. In cases of emergency, the doctors on staff in the hospital step in and transfer the patient to trauma rooms.
Some women have to be sent out of the community if it's medically necessary.
It's what happened to Tukkiapik during her first pregnancy.
Margaret Tukkiapik hopes each of the six other communities on the Ungava coast can have their own midwifery services. (Josianne Letourneau/CBC)
"I did not like that at all," she said.
"It's not how I was treated. It was just being away from home for so long, and then not knowing what to expect."
When she became pregnant with her daughter, in 2013, she said she took better care of herself — adamant that she wanted to stay home to deliver.
Doing things differently
Tukkiapik gave birth just down the hall from the current maternity ward, years before the unit created its own wing in the hospital.

Her daughter's birth was the first month Marilyn Mesher was on shift as a student, says Tukkiapik. Mesher later became the first Inuk from the Ungava coast to graduate from a midwifery program. She's now Tukkiapik's colleague.
"We're very proud," said Elena Mesher, Marilyn's sister.
Elena sat in a patient room in the maternity centre, holding her two-year-old son, Vincent — who was born at home, thanks to the help of the midwifery team, who also do house calls.
Elena Mesher delivered her son, Vincent, at home with the help of the midwives working in Kuujjuaq. (Josianne Letourneau/CBC)
"It's very important to have local midwives there with you because they understand what's going on," she said. "You can speak to them in your own language."
That's a sticking point for Tukkiapik.

Walking down the maternity ward's hallway, lined with parenting and newborn pamphlets, she pointed into some of the birthing rooms — whose doors have a notice posted on the outside: "Thank you for speaking Inuktitut or English in this room."

items: Changing childbirth in Nunavut: Arviat Cultural Safety Project plots a new path for midwifery in the territory

blocks.text: "Everyone's most comfortable in their first language," she said.
"If they don't understand, they will not ask you … But when you talk to them in their own language, they understand more and [are] able to ask for better care."
When appointments are done in Inuktitut, she says patients also have a better understanding of the level of care they should be receiving.
Piles of pamphlets are available at the maternity clinic, which is connected to Kuujjuaq's hospital centre. (Rachel Watts/CBC)
It's part of why both Tukkiapik and Annanack-Lauzon want to see their small ward expand.
Kuujjuaq's maternity centre began developing in the '80s. Decades later, they're still doing things differently.
In one of its two delivery rooms is a double bed — much bigger than a standard hospital bed, and made for women who want family members or partners close to them while they labour.
"We don't ask them to just be laying on their back as they're delivering. They can deliver in whatever position they're comfortable," said Tukkiapik.
Just to the right of the room is the centre's bulletin board, lined with babies' footprints, names and birth details — posted as a reminder of every child born in the ward in the calendar year.
"When it's a new year, we'll put them in a binder and start our new footprint collection," she said.
Talks of expansion

For over 40 years, the fertility rate in Nunavik has remained nearly twice as high as the Quebec average, according to a 2021 health profile of the region by the Nunavik Board of Health and Social Services.

In Kuujjuaq's maternity centre, deliveries over the past 10 to 15 years have also increased, and now the centre — consisting of the two birthing rooms and a few consultation rooms on the hospital's first floor — sees an average of 100 births every year, says Larry Watt, the executive director of the health centre.
"Our space … is very limited," said Watt.
Larry Watt, the executive director of the Ungava Tulattavik Health Centre, says there are plans to expand the midwifery building. (Josianne Letourneau/CBC)

But he says there's a plan to get a bigger facility in the next few years to offer more services, in part because the ward also takes on births, prenatal and postpartum care from neighbouring villages along the Ungava Coast.
Just next door to the maternity wing is the Maison de Transit, a temporary housing facility for the patients and family members from isolated communities who are flown in for care.
But for Tukkiapik, she dreams of a time when each of the 6 other communities on the Ungava coast have their own midwifery services.
"'Cause it makes a big difference," she said. "Each community must fight to have their own."
Annanack-Lauzon agreed, encouraging more Inuit to join.
"That's what we want," she said, cradling her baby bump. "It's really, really, awesome that we get to have this care."
